description: Biz tutkulu geliştiriciler ve üreticileri oluşan tam kadro bir takımız.Temel uzmanlık alanımız otonom sistemler, yapay zeka ve IoT,Python,Flutter ve mikrodenetleyicilerde sahip olduğumuz güçlü geçmiş sayesinde donanım ve yazılım birleştirme uzmanız.NASA Space Apps Challenge 'da işlevsel projeler üretmek ve inovasyonun sınırlarını zorlamak için burdayız.
summary: When an astronaut enters a complaint (e.g., "my stomach hurts"), the application marks the corresponding area on a human body figure. If 3 out of the 4 crew members report similar complaints, a collective alert appears on the screen. Using a rule-based algorithm, the application combines these complaints with actual NASA blood test data—such as hemoglobin/hematocrit, calcium levels, or inflammatory markers like CRP—to provide clues as to which organ or muscle group might be affected. For any values ​​that fall outside the normal range, the system suggests "potentially related conditions," and for minor issues, it offers simple, evidence-based recommendations to follow until communication with Earth is re-established. Each astronaut has their own personal dashboard; individual complaints are aggregated into a single dataset, which is then used to generate a prioritized list of health concerns upon the crew's return to Earth. The entire system operates without an internet connection and does not rely on artificial intelligence.
details:
offline decision-support dashboard that helps an astronaut interpret blood results and symptoms when contact with Earth is delayed or lost, as on future Moon and Mars missions.

What it does and how it works: The astronaut taps the painful area on a front/back body map and enters severity, duration and symptoms. The app compares each blood marker with its reference range and with the person’s own pre-flight values (red = out of range, yellow = within range but at least 20% away from the pre-flight average, green = normal). Each complaint is then ranked with a transparent, rule-based urgency score (3×severity + 2×duration + repeat + 2×blood signal + 2×crew + red flag) into Urgent, High, Medium or Watch. The app shows possible related conditions with evidence levels, practical steps, and when the flight surgeon should be notified. If two or more crew members report problems in the same body region within 48 hours, it raises a crew-pattern alert with a checklist of possible shared causes (food, water, equipment). The reasoning behind every score is shown on screen.

Benefits and intended impact: The tool helps a crew member who is not a physician decide what to look at first and when to escalate, without any connection. It can reveal a shared cause that would otherwise go unnoticed. It runs fully offline and no data leaves the device. We aim to support safer, faster and more autonomous medical decisions on deep-space missions. The same approach could also help in other low-connectivity settings such as polar stations, ships or disaster areas.

Tools and technologies: Plain JavaScript, HTML/CSS and SVG in a single self-contained file. There are no frameworks, servers or network calls, and it runs in any modern browser without special hardware. Settings and entries are stored locally in the browser. Blood data is real: NASA OSDR studies OSD-575 and OSD-569 (Inspiration4, four civilian astronauts, samples before and after flight), prepared into a compact structure embedded in the app. Complaints in the demo are simulated.

Creativity: The tool combines blood data, symptoms, an interactive body map and crew-level pattern detection in one offline, explainable dashboard. It also includes a guided demo mode that walks through a full scenario.

Factors our team considered:

  • Safety: the app does not diagnose and never suggests drugs, doses or supplements. The flight surgeon makes the final decision.
  • Explainability: we chose a rule-based approach instead of machine learning because four astronauts are too few to train a reliable model, and every decision must be auditable.
  • Evidence: recommendations are labeled by evidence level (peer-reviewed finding, agency source, general medical knowledge).
  • Honest limits: reference ranges are Earth adult ranges, and the thresholds (20% deviation, score cut-offs, crew rules) are team assumptions that need validation with flight surgeons. The dataset contains no in-flight blood draws.
